text: I finally managed to ___ the final level of the game.
why: gaming sense 'beat a level' not covered by hint (hint: win a game); 'win the level' also said

text: Nobody can ___ my grandmother's apple pie.
why: idiom 'nothing beats X' (= is better than), not covered by hint

text: Two ___ held up the post office last week.
why: needs plural 'robbers'; 'Two robber' is ungrammatical

text: The company pays a good ___ plus a bonus.
why: no time cue; 'a good wage plus a bonus' equally correct

text: Her ___ increases every January.
why: no time cue; 'her wage increases' equally correct

text: The manager's ___ is higher than a clerk's.
why: no time cue; 'wage' also acceptable

text: Could you ___ me your bike for the day?
why: PAIR-LEVEL: 'loan' as a verb (= lend) is standard American English

text: He asked his brother to ___ him a hundred euros.
why: PAIR-LEVEL: 'loan him a hundred euros' is standard (esp. AmE)

text: Please ___ me your umbrella until Monday.
why: PAIR-LEVEL: 'loan' verb (AmE) also fits

text: I can ___ you my notes if you like.
why: PAIR-LEVEL: 'loan' verb (AmE) also fits

text: Never ___ more than you can afford to lose.
why: PAIR-LEVEL: 'loan' verb also fits (money context makes it very natural)

text: Would your parents ___ you money for the course?
why: PAIR-LEVEL: 'loan you money' is standard (esp. AmE)

text: My friend agreed to ___ me his tent for the trip.
why: PAIR-LEVEL: 'loan' verb (AmE) also fits

text: He never wants to ___ his tools.
why: PAIR-LEVEL: 'loan' verb fits; 'borrow his tools' also possible if 'his' = someone else

text: Can you ___ me your phone for a quick call?
why: PAIR-LEVEL: 'loan' verb (AmE) also fits

text: The signing of the peace deal was a ___ event.
why: 'historical event' (an event in history) is also a standard collocation

text: The museum has a ___ map of the city from 1800.
why: 'historic map' (old, surviving from the past) is very common

text: Archaeologists look for ___ evidence in old documents.
why: content error: archaeologists dig; historians study documents

text: The café has a ___ photo exhibition about old trams.
why: 'historic photos' common; sentence awkward

text: We learned about the ___ of the old castle.
why: 'the story of the old castle' also natural

text: The ___ of the telephone starts in the nineteenth century.
why: 'The story of the telephone starts...' fully natural

text: That is a sad ___, but it has a happy end.
why: 'happy end' is a Russianism; English says 'happy ending'

text: The tour guide explained the ___ of the bridge.
why: 'explained the story of the bridge' also acceptable

text: Leave the room ___ you found it.
why: 'like' as a conjunction is common informal standard (esp. AmE)

text: He speaks English ___ a native speaker.
why: 'as a native speaker' (= being one) also correct, different meaning

text: She has learned Spanish ___ last year.
why: unnatural tense: 'has been learning' needed with since

text: Happy birthday! Same to you, ___!
why: illogical reply to 'Happy birthday'; 'Same to you, too' is redundant

text: This cake was made ___ for your birthday.
why: 'made especially for you' is standard (dictionaries list this sense)

text: I came here ___ to see you.
why: 'came especially to see you' is standard

text: He wrote this song ___ for his daughter.
why: 'especially for his daughter' is standard

text: This app is ___ made for students who learn English.
why: 'especially made for' also used; overlap of purpose sense

text: I was not ___ hungry after lunch.
why: 'not specially hungry' is normal British English

text: Don't worry; it is not ___ difficult.
why: 'not specially difficult' is normal British English

text: Thank you, ___ for your help last week.
why: unnatural comma/structure; reads oddly with either word

text: It is a ___ road with no houses or shops.
why: lonely = remote/isolated place, a meaning not in the hint

text: He wrote a poem about a ___ tree on a hill.
why: lonely = isolated (poetic), not 'sad without company'

text: The ___ lighthouse stood far from the shore.
why: lonely = isolated place, meaning not in the hint

text: A ___ cabin in the mountains was his home.
why: lonely = remote place, meaning not in the hint

text: There are ___ chairs left, so hurry up.
why: 'few' (almost none) clashes with 'hurry up' (needs 'only a few'); 'little chairs' = small chairs is grammatical

text: He made very ___ mistakes in the dictation.
why: 'very little mistakes' (= tiny mistakes) also grammatical, adjective sense

text: What ___ lovely weather we have today!
why: 'What such' is ungrammatical; correct is 'What lovely weather!'

text: The last bus has already ___.
why: BrE 'has already been' (= came and left) is also used

text: How long have you ___ in Slovakia?
why: 'been' = stayed (be), not the 'went and came back' sense in the hint

text: Have you heard their ___ song? It came out yesterday.
why: 'their last song' commonly means most recent too

text: I love the ___ film by that director; it just came to cinemas.
why: 'last film' commonly = most recent; hint 'the one before now' supports it

text: The ___ update fixed several bugs and was released this morning.
why: 'the last update' (most recent) is natural

text: The ___ edition of the magazine has a long interview.
why: 'last edition' (previous/most recent issue) also acceptable

text: The ___ fashion shows new colours for this autumn.
why: garden path: 'fashion shows' reads as a noun; awkward

text: The two friends help ___ other with homework.
why: 'each other' is a fixed reciprocal pronoun, not covered by the hint

text: They hugged ___ other at the station.
why: 'each other' is a fixed phrase, not covered by the hint

text: Take ___ of these pills after meals.
why: unnatural; normal is 'Take one pill after each meal'

text: You can visit us ___ now and then.
why: idiom 'every now and then', not covered by the hint
